I Come From Five Generations of Farmers. Here is Why I Stopped Trusting Almost Every Jar of Ghee Sold in India.

After I learned what really goes into most of them, I went back to my family's way of making it. Then I did the one thing almost no brand will do. I let you check every claim yourself.

By the Founder, ELIQO Naturals
Sponsored content · Updated today


Every week, someone tells me their family has eaten pure desi ghee for years. A relative who swears by a village brand. A neighbour who buys the most expensive tin on the shelf. A friend who is certain, absolutely certain, that the jar in her kitchen is the real thing.

Most of them are wrong.

And the hardest part is not that they are wrong. It is that they have no way to know it.

I do not say that to frighten anyone. I am not here to scare you out of your own kitchen. I say it because I spent my whole childhood inside the process that most brands only print on a label. I know the difference between ghee that is made and ghee that is assembled.

I know what it looks like when the milk is real. I know what a kitchen smells like when the butter is churned by hand. And I know, the very moment I lift the lid, when a jar is pretending to be something it is not.

I come from a farming family. Five generations of it.

Before me there was my mother. Before her, her mother. Back and back, to a time when nobody thought to ask whether the ghee was pure, because you had watched it being made with your own two eyes.

I grew up watching milk become curd, curd become butter, and butter become ghee. By hand. The slow way. In my grandmother's kitchen, on a low flame, on a Sunday morning, with the smell of it filling every room in the house.

There was no label to trust back then. There was only the process, and the people who did it, and the smell that told you it was done right.

So I know exactly what real ghee is supposed to smell like. And I know, with the kind of certainty that only comes from childhood, that most of what is sold today is not that.

For years, though, I bought mine the way you probably do. From shops. From premium brands. Beautiful jars. Confident words on the front. Traditional. Pure. A2. Bilona. I trusted the label, because what else is there to trust?

Then I started reading about how ghee actually moves through the market in this country. And what I found is the reason I could not go back.

In 2024, the ghee supplied to one of the most protected temple kitchens in the country was found to be adulterated.

The ghee used at Tirupati, of all places, failed its lab tests. The contract was terminated.

Sit with that for a moment. This is an institution with its own laboratories. Its own procurement committees. Priests and officials whose entire job is to protect what goes into a prasadam eaten by millions of people.

And even they were supplied fake ghee.

So I asked myself a very simple question. If they could be fooled, with all of that behind them, then what chance did my family have? What chance did any of us have, standing in a supermarket aisle, holding a jar, reading a label written by the very people selling it?

What I Found When I Followed the Ghee Back to the Farm

So I did what a farmer's child is trained to do. I stopped reading labels and I followed the ghee backwards, all the way to where it is supposed to come from.

What I found was not a shortage of pure ghee. It was something worse than that.

There is no shortage of pure ghee. There is a shortage of any way to prove it.

I learned that anonymous drums of pale yellow fat move quietly through trade channels, and that smaller packers buy them and print aspirational words on the outside.

I learned that fat from one animal can be routed, relabelled, and sold as another.

I learned that the word Bilona has a cheaper cousin. It is called Bilona-style. And it is very often just a shortcut wearing the costume of the real thing.

And I learned the one fact that explains all of it. Genuine A2 milk is expensive, and it is slow. So anything sold cheap, in large volume, almost mathematically cannot be what it claims to be.

The problem, I finally understood, was never that honest ghee did not exist. Honest ghee exists. My grandmother made it.

The problem was that a family standing in a shop had no way on earth to tell the honest jar from the costume standing right next to it.

The answer was not a better promise. Every brand already makes the promise.

The answer was proof. Real proof. The kind a family can check for themselves, before they spend a single rupee.

Not purity you are asked to believe. Purity you can verify.

That Is How ELIQO A2 Gir Bilona Ghee Was Born

So I stopped buying ghee altogether. And I went back to making it, the way my family always had, with exactly one modern promise added on top.

Everything I could not verify as a customer, I decided to show you as a founder.

What Changed in My Own Kitchen

The first thing that changed was not in my body. It was in my head.

The first morning I cooked with our own ghee, I did something I had not done in years. I stopped wondering.

I did not turn the jar over and read the back with suspicion. I did not stand there comparing prices, quietly trying to guess which brand was lying the least. I did not need to. I already knew. I had seen the cows. I had seen the churn. I had read the report with my own eyes.

My mother noticed the smell before she noticed anything else.

She walked into the kitchen, stopped, and said it took her back forty years. To her own mother's kitchen. To a Sunday morning long before any of this.

That smell was the entire benchmark I had spent months chasing. And there it was, at last, in a single warm spoon.

My children ate it on hot rice, with nothing else on the plate, and asked for more. And the smallest thing of all told me it was finally working.

Nobody in the house kept a second trusted jar hidden at the back of the shelf anymore. The one you keep for the days you do not quite believe the jar in front.

That is the quiet thing honest ghee gives a home. Not a promise. The end of second-guessing.

Why I Cannot Make It Faster

I will be honest about the one part of this that frustrates people.

I cannot make this quickly.

Real Bilona is hand-churned in small batches. Genuine Gir A2 milk is limited by how many cows there are, and by how carefully they are kept. There is a ceiling on how much honest ghee one kitchen can make, and I have chosen to live under it.

I could triple the output tomorrow. I know exactly how. I would simply do what the rest of the market does. Blend it. Buy anonymous fat by the drum. Call a shortcut Bilona-style and hope nobody reads the label too closely.

I built this brand for the single purpose of never doing that. So when a batch sells out, the next one is genuinely a little while away. It cannot be rushed without becoming the exact thing I walked away from.

The limit is not a marketing tactic. The limit is the proof.

My Promise to You

The Grandmother's Promise. We will never sell you a jar we would not cook for our own children. Every batch is hand-churned from genuine Gir cow milk, smelled and checked by us before it is sealed, and carries a lab report you can read. No anonymous fat. No Bilona-style shortcut. No word we cannot back with proof.

I can make a promise that bold for one simple reason. I have already smelled every batch myself, before it ever left for your door.

The only people who cannot make a promise like this one are the people who already know what is really in their jar.

The Bottom Line

You have two options here. They are honest ones, so I will lay them out plainly.

You can keep buying ghee the way most of India does. Trusting the label. Hoping the jar in front of you is the honest one. Never quite sure, always keeping a second jar at the back of the shelf for the days you do not believe the first.

Or you can buy one jar where every single claim on it is something you can check for yourself, backed by a lab report you can read before you spend a single rupee.

I built ELIQO because I wanted exactly that for my own family. It is the same thing, unchanged, that I am now offering yours.

Warm a spoon. Let your nose decide. That was always the only test that ever mattered.
